questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant has a 1 day history of right-sided facial weakness that has worsened over several hours. She cannot raise her right eyebrow or close her right eye. Her right ear canal and pinna are normal. Limb power and sensation are normal. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute isolated LMN CN VII palsy with a normal ear is Bell's palsy, and pregnancy is its strongest risk factor. Stroke would spare the forehead.

steps.x: A diagnosis question about facial weakness in pregnancy: decide UMN or LMN first.

clues: ear canal and pinna are normal
Limb power and sensation are normal
steps.x: Forehead involved = **LMN**. Acute onset, normal ear, nothing else neurological, and **pregnancy** is the strongest risk factor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Isolated acute LMN facial palsy in pregnancy: **Bell's palsy**.

elim: No seizures, normal BP and no proteinuria.
GBS gives ascending limb weakness and often bilateral facial palsy.
Stroke spares the forehead; her eyebrow is weak.
Ramsay Hunt needs vesicles in the ear; the ear is normal.

steps.x: **A. Bell's palsy.** Pregnancy + whole-face weakness + normal ear = Bell's.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has a 2 day history of left-sided facial weakness. He had an ache behind his left ear before it began. He has no rash and no other neurological symptoms. On examination the left side of his face is weak, including the forehead.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Flattening of the left nasolabial fold
Left ptosis with a dilated pupil
questions.e: Bell's palsy weakens all the left facial muscles, flattening the nasolabial fold and drooping the mouth. Ptosis is CN III and facial numbness is CN V.

steps.x: It asks for an examination finding, so name the condition then its signs.
Postauricular ache, no rash, whole-face weakness: **Bell's palsy** (left CN VII LMN).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: LMN CN VII signs on the left: droop, lagophthalmos, **loss of the nasolabial fold**.

elim: Ptosis with a dilated pupil is CN III, not CN VII.
Facial sensation is CN V; Bell's is purely CN VII.
Tongue deviation is a CN XII sign.
Bell's affects the ipsilateral (left) face, not the opposite side.

steps.x: **A. Flattening of the left nasolabial fold.** CN VII is motor to the face, so look for motor signs on the SAME side.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman was diagnosed with right-sided Bell's palsy 1 week ago. She has been using no eye treatment. She now has a gritty, sore right eye that waters. On examination she cannot fully close the right eyelid and a strip of cornea stays exposed when she tries.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her eye symptoms?
o: Herpes simplex infection of the cornea
Reduced corneal sensation from CN V
Tear film evaporation from incomplete eyelid closure
questions.e: Lagophthalmos lets the tear film evaporate, drying the cornea and causing exposure keratopathy. Watering is reflex tearing, not a duct problem.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: explain the eye finding in this Bell's patient.

clues: cannot fully close the right eyelid
a strip of cornea stays exposed
steps.x: **Lagophthalmos** leaves the cornea exposed and unprotected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The tear film evaporates from the exposed cornea, drying it: **exposure keratopathy**.

elim: A blocked duct causes watering but not a gritty, exposed cornea.
HSV keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer; the clue here is the exposed cornea.
Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye with haloes and a fixed pupil.
Bell's spares CN V; corneal sensation is intact.

steps.x: **E. Tear film evaporation from incomplete eyelid closure.** Lagophthalmos -> evaporation -> exposure keratopathy -> ulcer.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with atrial fibrillation and hypertension has noticed his left face drooping over the past day. He cannot wrinkle the left side of his forehead or close his left eye tightly. Limb power, speech and the other cranial nerves are normal. His pulse rate is 84 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 146/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Forehead weakness makes this a LMN lesion, so it is Bell's palsy despite his stroke risk factors. A stroke spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical supply.

steps.x: A diagnosis question where the risk factors push you towards stroke: check the forehead.

clues: cannot wrinkle the left side of his forehead
Limb power, speech and the other cranial nerves are normal
steps.x: Forehead weak = **LMN**. Isolated CN VII. The AF is a red herring.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Isolated LMN facial palsy: **Bell's palsy**.

elim: An acoustic neuroma causes gradual hearing loss first and a slowly progressive palsy.
A stroke is a UMN lesion and spares the forehead.
A parotid tumour gives slowly progressive weakness and a lump.
A TIA is UMN, sudden and resolves within 24 hours.

steps.x: **B. Bell's palsy.** Forehead involved = LMN = Bell's, whatever the vascular risk factors.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 1 day history of right-sided facial weakness. Her GP suspects Bell's palsy. She has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg. The GP examines her further before making the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most suggest a central cause rather than Bell's palsy?
o: Altered taste on the right of the tongue
Sounds seeming louder in the right ear
questions.e: Limb weakness is a red flag for a central (stroke) cause. Taste change, hyperacusis, tearing and postauricular pain all fit Bell's palsy.

steps.x: It asks which finding is a red flag against Bell's.
Vascular risk factors: look for the **red flags** of a central lesion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Red flags: forehead sparing, **limb weakness**, multiple cranial nerves.

elim: Altered taste is part of Bell's (chorda tympani).
Postauricular pain is a typical Bell's prodrome.
Hyperacusis is a Bell's feature (stapedius).
Excess tearing occurs in Bell's palsy.

steps.x: **E. Weakness of the right arm.** Limb weakness, forehead sparing or several cranial nerves = think stroke.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has woken with right-sided facial weakness involving his forehead and mouth. He has no rash, and limb power and the other cranial nerves are normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. He is diagnosed with Bell's palsy.
questions.q: Which symptom is most likely to have preceded the weakness?
o: Painful vesicles in the right ear
questions.e: Postauricular pain often precedes Bell's palsy by a day or two. Vesicles in the ear would make it Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

steps.x: It asks for the prodrome of Bell's palsy.
Typical Bell's: the classic prodrome is ear pain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Postauricular otalgia** often comes a day or two before the weakness.

elim: Diplopia suggests CN III, IV or VI, a red flag.
Vesicles point to Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
Thunderclap headache suggests subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Ascending tingling suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.x: **B. Pain behind the right ear.** Bell's prodrome = ache behind the ear, no vesicles.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has a 2 day history of left-sided facial weakness involving his forehead. He cannot close his left eye. There are no other neurological signs and the ear is normal. He has a 4 year history of a long-term condition treated with metformin and takes no other medicines.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of this condition?
questions.e: Diabetes increases the risk of Bell's palsy, along with pregnancy and recent viral illness. The others are not recognised risk factors.

steps.x: It asks for a risk factor, so name the condition first.
LMN palsy = **Bell's palsy**. Metformin means **diabetes**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Risk factors: pregnancy (strongest), **diabetes**, recent viral illness.

elim: Asthma is not a risk factor for Bell's palsy.
Gout is not linked to Bell's palsy.
Osteoarthritis is not a risk factor.
Psoriasis is not a risk factor.

steps.x: **B. Diabetes mellitus.** Bell's risk factors: pregnancy, diabetes, recent viral illness.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman had a sore throat and runny nose 10 days ago. Over the past day her right face has become weak. She cannot raise her right eyebrow, close her right eye or smile on the right. Limb power and reflexes are normal. There are no vesicles and she has not travelled or been bitten by a tick.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bell's palsy is linked to viral inflammation, and recent viral illness raises the risk. Normal reflexes and limbs rule out Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.x: A diagnosis question after a viral illness.

clues: sore throat and runny nose 10 days ago
not travelled or been bitten by a tick
steps.x: Recent **viral illness** then isolated LMN CN VII palsy, no other features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bell's palsy**, linked to viral inflammation.

elim: GBS follows infection too, but gives limb weakness and areflexia.
No tick bite or rash, and Lyme is often bilateral.
MS gives a UMN or relapsing pattern with other deficits.
No vesicles, so not VZV Ramsay Hunt.

steps.x: **A. Bell's palsy.** Recent viral illness + isolated LMN facial palsy = Bell's.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman is diagnosed with Bell's palsy affecting the whole of the left side of her face. She has no limb symptoms and her ear is normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. The doctor asks how the weakness came on.
questions.q: Which is the most likely time course of her weakness?
o: Fluctuating through the day, worse when tired
questions.e: Bell's palsy comes on acutely over hours to a couple of days, not instantly. Instant onset suggests stroke; months suggests a tumour.

steps.x: It asks about the onset of Bell's palsy.

clues: whole of the left side of her face
steps.x: Bell's is **acute but not sudden**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It develops over hours to a day or two.

elim: Fatigable weakness suggests myasthenia gravis.
Sudden onset suggests a vascular (stroke) cause.
Slow progression suggests a tumour, such as parotid.
This pattern suggests multiple sclerosis.

steps.x: **E. Worsening over 1 to 2 days.** Bell's = acute (hours to 2 days), not sudden, not slowly progressive.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a 1 day history of right facial weakness involving the forehead. He says food tastes metallic and loud noises are uncomfortable in his right ear. Hearing is otherwise normal. Otoscopy shows a normal ear canal and tympanic membrane with no vesicles. There are no other neurological signs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Altered taste and hyperacusis are CN VII features of Bell's palsy. A normal ear with no vesicles rules out otitis media and Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

steps.x: A diagnosis question: facial palsy with taste and hearing symptoms.

clues: normal ear canal and tympanic membrane with no vesicles
steps.x: LMN CN VII palsy plus altered taste and **hyperacusis**, normal ear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bell's palsy**: taste and hyperacusis come from CN VII branches.

elim: Otoscopy would show a bulging, red tympanic membrane.
Cholesteatoma causes chronic discharge and conductive hearing loss.
No vesicles on otoscopy.
Schwannoma gives gradual hearing loss and tinnitus, and the palsy comes late.

steps.x: **B. Bell's palsy.** Taste change + hyperacusis + normal ear = Bell's.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 1 day history of right-sided drooping of her mouth. She has hypertension. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. Limb power and speech are normal. Her GP wants to decide whether this is Bell's palsy or a stroke.
questions.q: Which examination finding would best support Bell's palsy?
o: Drooping of the right corner of the mouth
questions.e: The upper face has bilateral cortical supply, so a stroke spares the forehead but Bell's palsy does not. Mouth droop occurs in both.

steps.x: It asks which sign separates LMN from UMN facial weakness.
Both cause a droopy mouth; the **forehead** separates them.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bell's (LMN) weakens the forehead; stroke spares it.

elim: Mouth droop occurs with both UMN and LMN lesions.
Normal limbs do not exclude a small stroke.
Speech can be normal in both.
Symmetrical eyebrow raising is forehead sparing, a UMN (stroke) sign.

steps.x: **E. Weak right eyebrow raising.** Test the forehead: weak = Bell's, spared = stroke.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man has a 2 day history of facial weakness. He cannot raise his left eyebrow, close his left eye or smile on the left. The right side of his face moves normally. There are no limb or other cranial nerve signs and his ear is normal. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site and type of lesion?
o: Left facial nerve, lower motor neurone
Left internal capsule, upper motor neurone
Right facial nerve, lower motor neurone
Right motor cortex, upper motor neurone
questions.e: Whole-face weakness on the left is a left LMN facial nerve lesion, as in Bell's palsy. A UMN lesion gives contralateral weakness sparing the forehead.

steps.x: It asks site and type: decide UMN or LMN, then the side.

clues: The right side of his face moves normally
no limb or other cranial nerve signs
steps.x: Whole left face weak = **LMN** lesion of the **left** CN VII.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Left facial nerve, LMN (Bell's palsy).

elim: A UMN lesion would spare the forehead and give a contralateral (right) palsy.
NMJ disease is fatigable and usually bilateral.
A LMN lesion weakens the same side; his left is weak.
A cortical lesion would spare the forehead.

steps.x: **A. Left facial nerve, lower motor neurone.** LMN = ipsilateral whole face; UMN = contralateral lower face.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 1 day history of left-sided facial weakness affecting her forehead, eye and mouth. She had an ache behind her left ear the day before. There are no vesicles and no limb symptoms. Her GP diagnoses Bell's palsy and asks about other symptoms.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is she most likely to report?
o: Sounds seeming unusually loud in the left ear
questions.e: Bell's palsy can paralyse stapedius, causing hyperacusis. Hearing loss, vertigo, numbness or diplopia suggest another cause.

steps.x: It asks for an associated symptom of Bell's palsy.
Bell's affects all of CN VII, including the stapedius branch.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hyperacusis**: sounds seem too loud on the affected side.

elim: Diplopia is a red flag for other cranial nerves.
Sensorineural loss suggests a vestibular schwannoma.
Facial numbness is CN V, not Bell's.
Vertigo points to the vestibular system or Ramsay Hunt.

steps.x: **D. Sounds seeming unusually loud in the left ear.** Bell's extras: hyperacusis, taste change, dry or watery eye.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man had right-sided Bell's palsy diagnosed 2 weeks ago. He did not use the eye drops he was given. He now has a painful red right eye with blurred vision. He cannot close the right eye fully. Fluorescein is instilled and the eye is examined with a blue light.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on fluorescein examination?
questions.e: Lagophthalmos without eye protection causes exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration, which take up fluorescein. A dendritic ulcer is HSV keratitis.

steps.x: It asks for the finding of a Bell's complication.

clues: did not use the eye drops
cannot close the right eye fully
steps.x: Untreated **lagophthalmos** dries the exposed cornea.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Exposure keratopathy**, which can ulcerate: fluorescein stains the exposed cornea.

elim: A dendritic ulcer is HSV keratitis, not exposure.
Disc cupping is glaucoma and is not seen with fluorescein.
Hyphaema is blood in the anterior chamber after trauma.
A shallow chamber suggests angle-closure glaucoma.

steps.x: **D. Inferior corneal staining from exposure.** Lagophthalmos without eye care -> exposure keratopathy and corneal ulcer.

questions.stem: A 38 year old shop worker sees her GP with right-sided facial weakness involving the forehead for 1 day. She cannot fully close her right eye. The ear is normal and there are no limb or other cranial nerve signs. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. She asks which tests she needs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Bell's palsy is a clinical diagnosis and needs no routine imaging (NICE CKS). MRI is kept for atypical features.

steps.x: It asks which tests: name the diagnosis first.

clues: no limb or other cranial nerve signs
steps.x: Typical **Bell's palsy** with no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bell's is a **clinical diagnosis**; no routine imaging.

elim: CT is for suspected stroke; she has no central features.
There is no tick exposure, rash or bilateral palsy.
MRI is only for atypical features.
Not routine; they do not confirm Bell's.

steps.x: **E. No investigation is required.** Typical Bell's = clinical diagnosis, no tests.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has noticed his right face becoming weaker over the past 4 months. He now cannot close his right eye. He also has gradually worsening hearing in his right ear. There are no vesicles. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Varicella zoster PCR of the ear
questions.e: A slowly progressive palsy with hearing loss is atypical for Bell's palsy, so MRI brain excludes a structural cause such as a tumour. Typical Bell's needs no imaging.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnostic test in a palsy with atypical features.
Bell's is acute. **Slow progression** plus hearing loss is atypical.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Atypical: **MRI brain** to exclude a central or structural cause.

elim: Slow progression and hearing loss are atypical; Bell's must not be assumed.
CT shows the cerebellopontine angle and facial nerve poorly.
These do not show a structural cause.
There are no vesicles to swab.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain.** Atypical features (slow, progressive, other symptoms) = MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has right-sided LMN facial weakness for the second time this year. The first episode was diagnosed as Bell's palsy and recovered over 2 months. This episode began 2 days ago. There are no other neurological signs and the ear is normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Recurrent same-side facial palsy is atypical, so MRI brain looks for a structural lesion. Typical first-episode Bell's needs no imaging.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation in recurrent facial palsy.

clues: for the second time this year
steps.x: A **recurrent** same-side palsy is atypical for Bell's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain** to exclude a structural cause.

elim: CT does not show the facial nerve course well.
There are no meningitic or GBS features.
A recurrence on the same side is atypical and needs imaging.
Sarcoid is possible, but imaging comes first.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain.** Recurrent or atypical palsy = MRI brain.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has a 1 day history of left-sided facial weakness involving the forehead. He has had thirst and passing more urine for 2 months. There are no other neurological signs. His BMI is 33 kg/m2. Investigations:
questions.q: Which result is most relevant to his risk of this condition?
questions.e: His HbA1c of 71 mmol/mol shows diabetes, which increases the risk of Bell's palsy. The other results are normal.

steps.x: It asks which result explains his risk.
Bell's palsy with symptoms of **diabetes**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A raised HbA1c shows diabetes, a risk factor for Bell's.

elim: His ALT is normal.
His CRP is normal.
His creatinine is normal.
His sodium is normal.

steps.x: **D. HbA1c.** Diabetes is a Bell's risk factor; look for a high HbA1c.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman is referred with suspected Bell's palsy. She has a 2 day history of right facial weakness involving the forehead. She also has numbness of the right cheek and double vision on looking to the right. Limb power is normal. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Involvement of CN V and VI as well as CN VII is a red flag, so MRI brain is needed. Bell's palsy is an isolated CN VII palsy.

steps.x: It asks for an investigation in a facial palsy with other signs.

clues: double vision on looking to the right
steps.x: CN V and CN VI are also affected: **multiple cranial nerves** is a red flag.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain** to exclude a central or structural lesion.

elim: Several cranial nerves are involved, which is a red flag.
EMG does not show a central or structural cause.
Hearing is not the problem.
Serology does not explain multiple cranial nerve palsies.

steps.x: **C. MRI brain.** More than one cranial nerve = not Bell's until imaged.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man has a 1 day history of left-sided facial weakness involving the forehead. He had a cold sore last week. The ear is normal and there are no other neurological signs. His temperature is 36.9°C. He has read that Bell's palsy is caused by a virus and asks to be tested for it.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Bell's palsy is thought to be HSV-1 reactivation, but the diagnosis is clinical and no viral test is used. MRI is only for atypical cases.

steps.x: It asks about testing in typical Bell's.
Typical **Bell's palsy**. HSV-1 reactivation is the likely cause, but it is not tested.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clinical diagnosis**; no tests.

elim: Serology is not used; most adults are HSV-1 positive anyway.
There are no meningitic features.
Imaging is only for atypical features.
There are no features of sarcoidosis.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis without tests.** Bell's is clinical: no serology, no imaging.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has a 30 hour history of right-sided facial weakness involving the forehead. The ear is normal and there are no other neurological signs. He has no medical history. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. He can partly close his right eye.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Oral prednisolone started within 72 hours of onset is first-line for Bell's palsy (NICE CKS). Antivirals alone are not recommended.

steps.x: It asks for initial treatment, so check timing from onset.
Typical **Bell's palsy** within **72 hours**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral prednisolone** now.

elim: IV steroids are not used; oral is first-line.
Steroids within 72 hours improve recovery.
Antivirals alone are not first-line.
Physiotherapy does not replace steroids.

steps.x: **D. Oral prednisolone.** Bell's within 72 hours = oral prednisolone.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has had left-sided facial weakness involving the forehead for 6 days. She did not see a doctor sooner. The ear is normal and there are no other neurological signs. She cannot fully close her left eye. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Prednisolone is started within 72 hours of onset, so at 6 days the priority is eye protection. ENT referral is only if there is no improvement after 3 weeks.

steps.x: It asks for management: check the time since onset.

clues: cannot fully close her left eye
steps.x: Bell's palsy at **6 days**, past the 72 hour steroid window.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No steroid now; protect the eye.

elim: Antivirals alone are not used, and she is past the window.
Steroids help only when started within 72 hours; she is at 6 days.
ENT referral is for no improvement after 3 weeks.
There are no atypical features.

steps.x: **A. Eye protection and supportive care.** Prednisolone only within 72 hours; eye care always.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a 36 hour history of left-sided facial weakness. He has no movement at all of the left forehead, eye or mouth. The ear is normal with no vesicles and there are no other neurological signs. His facial function is graded (see item resources).

visual.title: House-Brackmann facial nerve grade
visual.label: Grade VI
visual.caption: Grade VI: no movement, a complete paralysis.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Oral prednisolone is first-line, and an antiviral such as valaciclovir may be added for severe complete paralysis. An antiviral alone is not recommended.

steps.x: It asks for initial treatment in a severe palsy.
Bell's palsy within 72 hours with **complete paralysis** (grade VI).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Prednisolone, and consider an **antiviral** in severe complete paralysis.

elim: IV antivirals alone are not used for Bell's.
He is within 72 hours and needs treatment.
Antivirals are never given without the steroid.
Surgery is not routine treatment.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone and valaciclovir.** Complete paralysis: steroid plus consider aciclovir or valaciclovir.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman started oral prednisolone for right-sided Bell's palsy yesterday. She cannot fully close her right eye, which feels dry by day. She uses lubricating drops in the day and asks what she should do for the eye overnight.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice for the night?
o: Lubricating ointment and taping the eyelid closed
No treatment, as the eye closes during sleep
questions.e: Eye ointment and taping the eyelid closed at night protect against exposure keratopathy. The eye does not close during sleep in Bell's palsy.

steps.x: It asks for eye care in Bell's palsy.

clues: cannot fully close her right eye
what she should do for the eye overnight
steps.x: **Lagophthalmos** risks exposure keratopathy at night.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ointment at night and tape the eye closed.

elim: There is no infection to treat.
Lagophthalmos persists in sleep.
Steroid drops do not protect an exposed cornea.
There is no herpetic keratitis.

steps.x: **B. Lubricating ointment and taping the eyelid closed.** Drops by day, ointment and taping at night.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man was diagnosed with left-sided Bell's palsy 4 weeks ago and took oral prednisolone within 48 hours. He has used eye care. His facial weakness has not improved at all. There are no new neurological signs. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: If Bell's palsy shows no improvement after 3 weeks, refer urgently to ENT to look for another cause. A repeat steroid course is not used.

steps.x: It asks the next step for a palsy that has not improved.
**No improvement after 3 weeks**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent ENT referral**.

elim: Botulinum is for later synkinesis, not this stage.
Waiting delays diagnosis of an alternative cause.
A repeat steroid course is not recommended.
Antivirals are only an early add-on.

steps.x: **E. Urgent ENT referral.** No recovery at 3 weeks = urgent ENT.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman arrives at the GP surgery 1 hour after her right face dropped. Her receptionist thinks it is Bell's palsy. She can raise both eyebrows equally, but her right mouth droops and her right arm drifts. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 168/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Forehead sparing and limb weakness are red flags for a central cause, so she needs emergency stroke assessment. Prednisolone is only for true Bell's palsy.

steps.x: It asks the next step: check for red flags first.
**Forehead sparing** and **limb weakness** are red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Think stroke: emergency transfer.

elim: There is no eye closure problem; this is not Bell's.
Red flags mean this is not Bell's palsy.
Delay would miss the stroke treatment window.
This is an emergency, not a routine scan.

steps.x: **A. Emergency transfer for stroke assessment.** Red flags in suspected Bell's = treat as stroke.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 24 hour history of right-sided facial weakness involving the forehead. The ear is normal and there are no other neurological signs. His capillary glucose is 9.2 mmol/L. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Defer treatment until diabetes is controlled
questions.e: Oral prednisolone within 72 hours is still first-line in diabetes, with closer glucose monitoring. Deferring loses the treatment window.

steps.x: It asks for initial treatment in a patient with diabetes.
Bell's palsy within 72 hours; diabetes is a risk factor, not a contraindication.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral prednisolone, with closer glucose monitoring.

elim: Delay would miss the 72 hour window.
IV antivirals are not used for Bell's.
Physiotherapy does not replace steroids.
Topical steroids have no role.

steps.x: **C. Oral prednisolone with glucose monitoring.** Diabetes: still give prednisolone, watch the sugars.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman was diagnosed with right-sided Bell's palsy 2 weeks ago and completed a course of prednisolone. She can now close her right eye with effort and her smile is slightly better. She uses drops by day and ointment at night. There are no new symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue eye care and expect gradual recovery
questions.e: She is improving, which is the usual course of Bell's palsy, so she should continue eye care. Urgent ENT referral is for no improvement after 3 weeks.

steps.x: It asks the next step in a recovering palsy.
Improving at 2 weeks: the natural course.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Continue eye protection; most recover over weeks to months.

elim: There are no atypical features and she is improving.
Repeat steroids are not recommended.
Antivirals are only an early add-on.
ENT referral is for no improvement after 3 weeks; she is improving.

steps.x: **A. Continue eye care and expect gradual recovery.** Improving = carry on eye care; no improvement at 3 weeks = ENT.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has a 1 day history of left-sided facial weakness involving her forehead. She had an ache behind her left ear the day before. There are no ear vesicles, no tick exposure and no other neurological signs. She is diagnosed with Bell's palsy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.e: Bell's palsy is thought to be due to HSV-1 reactivation inflaming the facial nerve. VZV reactivation causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome with vesicles.

steps.x: It asks the cause of Bell's palsy.
Bell's is thought to be viral.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HSV-1 reactivation** inflaming the facial nerve.

elim: That is Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Lyme needs tick exposure.
Pontine ischaemia gives other brainstem signs.
VZV gives Ramsay Hunt with vesicles.

steps.x: **C. Herpes simplex virus type 1 reactivation.** Bell's = HSV-1; Ramsay Hunt = VZV.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has Bell's palsy affecting the whole right side of his face. His doctor explains that the facial nerve is inflamed. He asks why mild inflammation of one nerve can cause such marked weakness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the weakness?
o: Swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal
Viral destruction of the facial muscles
questions.e: The inflamed facial nerve swells inside the narrow bony facial canal and is compressed, giving LMN weakness of the whole ipsilateral face.

steps.x: It asks the mechanism of weakness in Bell's palsy.
The nerve swells in a tight space.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Swelling within the **narrow bony facial canal** compresses the nerve.

elim: That is myasthenia gravis.
A central lesion would spare the forehead.
Infarction is vascular, not inflammatory.
The muscles are normal; the nerve is affected.

steps.x: **D. Swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal.** Inflamed nerve + rigid canal = compression = LMN weakness.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman has left-sided Bell's palsy. She cannot wrinkle the left side of her forehead. A medical student notes that patients with a stroke and facial droop can still raise their eyebrows.
questions.q: Which best explains why her forehead is weak?
o: Her lesion is distal to the nucleus, after the bilateral cortical input
Her oculomotor nerve is also affected
Her trigeminal nerve is also affected
The forehead receives only contralateral cortical input
The lesion is in the right motor cortex
questions.e: The upper face has bilateral cortical supply, so a stroke spares the forehead. Bell's damages the nerve after this input, weakening the whole side.

steps.x: It asks for the anatomy behind forehead involvement.

clues: cannot wrinkle the left side of her forehead
steps.x: The upper face has **bilateral cortical innervation**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A LMN lesion of the nerve cuts every fibre to that side, so the forehead is weak too.

elim: CN III moves the eyelid, not the forehead.
CN V is sensory to the face, not motor to the forehead.
The forehead receives BILATERAL cortical input.
A cortical lesion spares the forehead.

steps.x: **A. Her lesion is distal to the nucleus, after the bilateral cortical input.** Bilateral cortical supply protects the forehead only from UMN lesions.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has a 2 day history of right-sided LMN facial weakness. He says sweet and salty foods taste odd on the front of his tongue. Sensation of the face and tongue is normal. There are no vesicles and no other neurological signs.
questions.q: Which nerve branch is most likely responsible for his altered taste?
questions.e: The chorda tympani branch of CN VII carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue. CN IX supplies the posterior third.

steps.x: It asks which branch explains the taste change.

clues: Sensation of the face and tongue is normal
steps.x: Taste on the **anterior two thirds** of the tongue is CN VII.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Carried by the **chorda tympani**.

elim: CN IX carries taste from the posterior third.
This supplies the lacrimal gland, not taste on the tongue.
CN XII is motor to the tongue.
CN X carries taste from the epiglottis.

steps.x: **A. Chorda tympani.** Anterior 2/3 taste = chorda tympani (CN VII).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman was diagnosed with Bell's palsy yesterday and has started oral prednisolone. She has no other medical history. She is worried that her face will stay like this permanently and asks what usually happens.
questions.q: Which is the most likely outcome?
o: Progressive weakness spreading to the other side
questions.e: Most cases of Bell's palsy resolve over weeks to months as the nerve inflammation settles. Recovery within 24 hours describes a TIA.

steps.x: It asks about prognosis.
Bell's is self-limiting.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Most resolve over **weeks to months**.

elim: Most recover; permanent weakness is uncommon.
Bell's does not spread; this would suggest GBS.
Surgery is not needed for most.
That is the timescale of a TIA.

steps.x: **E. Resolution over weeks to months.** Bell's usually resolves over weeks to months.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has Bell's palsy. His facial function was scored at each clinic visit, shown as a percentage of normal movement (see item resources). He had no further treatment after a course of prednisolone.

visual.title: Facial movement over time
visual.caption: Steady recovery over weeks to months without further treatment.

questions.q: Which best explains the pattern of recovery?
o: Collateral supply from the opposite facial nerve
Inflammation and compression of the nerve subsiding
The trigeminal nerve taking over facial movement
questions.e: Bell's palsy recovers as the inflammation and compression within the facial canal subside. The cortex and muscles are not affected.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism of recovery.
Function improves gradually over weeks without further treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The inflamed, compressed nerve recovers as swelling settles.

elim: Each facial nerve supplies only its own side.
The muscles were never damaged.
The cortex is not involved in Bell's.
CN V cannot take over facial movement.

steps.x: **B. Inflammation and compression of the nerve subsiding.** Recovery follows the swelling going down in the facial canal.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a 1 day history of right-sided Bell's palsy and is prescribed oral prednisolone. There are no other neurological signs and the ear is normal. She asks how a steroid tablet can help a nerve problem, and why it must be started quickly.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of benefit?
o: It blocks acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction
It improves blood flow to the motor cortex
It reduces swelling of the nerve in the facial canal
It stimulates regrowth of the facial muscles
questions.e: Prednisolone reduces inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve in the bony canal, so it works best within 72 hours. It has no antiviral action.

steps.x: It asks how prednisolone works in Bell's palsy.

clues: why it must be started quickly
steps.x: The damage comes from inflammation compressing the nerve.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Steroids reduce **nerve swelling** in the canal, best early (within 72 hours).

elim: That is pyridostigmine, used in myasthenia.
Bell's is not a cortical problem.
Steroids are not antiviral.
The muscles are not damaged.

steps.x: **D. It reduces swelling of the nerve in the facial canal.** Steroids work early by reducing swelling in the canal.
